newsitem.title: RUSSIA: De Beers says Russia deal in Yeltsin hands.
newsitem.headline: De Beers says Russia deal in Yeltsin hands.

text.p: A stalled gem export deal between Russia's Almazy Rossii-Sakha diamond monopoly and De Beers is in the hands of ailing President Boris Yeltsin, with no possible signing date in sight, a top De Beers official said on Tuesday.
Raymond Clark, general director of De Beers' Moscow representation, told Reuters it was unclear when a trade agreement could be signed.
"It would be a foolish person to speculate when President Boris Yeltsin is going to sign a decree," he said. "I'm not in a position to predict when that might be."
Yeltsin has spent most of the last six months away from the Kremlin with heart problems, for which he had major surgery in November 1996, and now with pneumonia.
Clark said the text of the agreement awaiting Yeltsin's signature was unchanged from a draft accord reached in September 1996 and based upon a February 1996 memorandum of understanding.
The memoramdum replaced a five-year formal deal that expired in December 1995.
"We haven't been involved in any discussion about a reworked agreement from the situation that we left off in September," Clarke said.
But he said that questions over the legality of the draft agreement under Russian constitutional law meant that Yeltsin was now the key player in the stalled deal's fate.
"There were legal questions relating to whether or not the memorandum breached some aspects of the Russian constitution," he said.
Yeltsin has wide-ranging powers under Russia's new, post-communist constitution.
De Beers stopped all purchases of diamonds from Russia on December 31, 1996 when it cancelled its interim arrangement after the Russian authorities failed to approve or reject a draft new trade deal.

Clarke said that ministries -- including the Finance Ministry, whose head, Alexander Livshits, told Russian news agencies last month that he wanted the deal reworked -- had approved the draft deal and sent it to Yeltsin's administration for perusal and signature.
Officials had said last year that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was responsible for signing off on the deal.
